# un-a76380-shaheed-2021-freedom-of-thought
- **URL:** https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n21/274/90/pdf/n2127490.pdf (official English PDF, reached via https://docs.un.org/en/A/76/380) ; UN Digital Library record https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3945858 returned 403 · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v1 drafting, claim C17
- **What it establishes:** A/76/380, "Interim report of the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief, Ahmed Shaheed — Freedom of thought," General Assembly, 76th session, distributed 5 October 2021 (28 pp.). The Summary and para. 25 set out four attributes; Section VI.B "Surveillance that infers thought" (paras 52–54) treats inferential surveillance as a threat; para. 54 cites Penney's Wikipedia chilling-effects study (fn 102) for the claim that surveilled people change what they read. Para. 16 discusses "extended cognition" and whether search histories may constitute thought. Para. 7 describes the report as "the first attempt to comprehensively articulate the right's content and scope in the United Nations system."
- **Key passages:** Summary: "he first examines four proposed attributes of this right: (a) freedom not to disclose one's thoughts; (b) freedom from punishment for one's thoughts; (c) freedom from impermissible alteration of one's thoughts; and (d) an enabling environment for freedom of thought." Para. 25: "(a) not being forced to reveal one's thoughts; (b) no punishment and/or sanctions for one's thoughts; (c) no impermissible alteration of one's thoughts; and (d) States fostering an enabling environment for freedom of thought." Para. 27: "as technological advances increase the possibility of accurately decoding or inferring one's inner mind accurately, clear parameters and protections for forum internum rights need urgent consideration." Para. 52: "surveillance technologies deployed in 'counter-terrorism' and national security apparatuses threaten freedom of thought, where they purport to reveal one's thoughts through inference". Para. 54: "Research suggests that individuals modify their behaviour when they know that they are subject to surveillance, including through self-censorship. Some suggest that when surveillance thoroughly infiltrates rights holders' digital lives, they not only censor what they write, but also censor with whom they associate, what they read and, ultimately, alter what they think." (fn 101: catalogofbias.org Hawthorne effect; fn 102: lawcat.berkeley.edu/record/1127413 = Penney 2016, pp. 164 and 169.) Para. 16: "stakeholders submit that 'thought' is not simply limited to what is inside one's mind, but encompasses so-called 'extended cognition' or 'external thinking'. They theorize that certain objects (e.g., diaries, notebooks) or aspects of one's 'digital footprint' (e.g., Internet search histories, smartphone contents) may constitute 'thought'". Para. 18: "While freedom of thought is absolute, freedom of expression can be limited."
- **Reliability:** Primary UN document (official PDF). A Special Rapporteur report is expert opinion transmitted by the Secretary-General, not a treaty-body interpretation; it says so itself ("does not conclusively resolve debates").
- **Relevance to this project:** C17, and the bridge to C22 (the report itself relies on Penney). Note the report says "what they read"; "search" appears in para. 16 (search histories as possible thought), not in para. 54.
